library(readr)

# Data Sets
```{r}

# 1. Course Data
course_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wkessler-oss/PGA-Tour-ML-Analysis/main/Course%20Data.csv"
course_data <- read_csv(course_url)

# 2. Player Data
master_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wkessler-oss/PGA-Tour-ML-Analysis/main/PGA_2025_Master.csv"
pga_master <- read_csv(master_url)

pga_master <- pga_master %>%
  mutate(
    # Clean to_par
    to_par = case_when(
      to_par == "E" ~ "0",
      TRUE ~ to_par
    ),
    to_par = as.numeric(to_par),
    
    # Convert all round scores and total to numeric
    r1    = as.numeric(r1),
    r2    = as.numeric(r2),
    r3    = as.numeric(r3),
    r4    = as.numeric(r4),
    total = as.numeric(total)
  )

# Make sure it came in correctly
head(course_data)
head(pga_master)
```
### Dimensions
```{r}
dim(course_data)
dim(pga_master)
```
The player dataset contains 1,755 rows and 19 columns. Each row represents one player’s participation in a particular tournament during the 2025 season. The columns describe the player, tournament, course, finishing position, individual round scores, total score, score relative to par, and strokes-gained performance. Players appear in multiple rows because they compete in multiple tournaments.

The course dataset contains 111 rows and 32 columns. Each row represents a golf course or a specific course setup, since some courses have separate entries for different events or par configurations. The columns describe course characteristics and playing statistics, including par, yardage, adjusted scoring, adjusted driving distance, driving accuracy, fairway width, and greens in regulation.

## Data Set Descriptions

### Player Data

The dataset comes from official PGA Tour performace tacking sustems, which come from ShotLink. This is a swing data collection from high speed cameras, and other ,easurements on every hole. This Data is from the 2024-2025 PGA tour season, and includes Driving Distance, Green in Regulation, Strokes gained, and results. 

### Assumptions

We assume that the season averages of a players swing will be consistent week to week, not intaking the varience within it
This can be a risk becuase they could be injured or just fatigued from the season. Meaning that our dataset would not accuretly predict the cut.

Another assumption is that the players metrics are inherit to the player, and not to the course.
This is a risk becasue ofgten time players will be more comfortable on a course if they have played it more, or they will play more aggressive if they know the course.

### Course Data

The course data is from a PGA tour website, which analyses the courses architecture. It includes yardages, par, grass types, and other things like distance and hazards. 

### Assumptions
We assume that the courses do not chainge, such as the tee boxes do not move, and they do not change any hazards or conditions. 
This assumption is risky because conditions on tournament days can be super variable. THings such as wind and humidity can affect the way a ball flies immensely.

Another assuumption is that course paramteters affect all players the same
This is a risk because condition changes on a course may affect short vs long hitters very differently.

## Looking For Outliers
```{r}
pga_master %>%
  select(r1, r2, r3, r4, total, to_par, sg_total, sg_ott, sg_app, sg_arg, sg_putt, sg_rounds) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(value)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value, fill = variable)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 4) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Variable Distributions (Histograms)",
    subtitle = "Examine distribution shape, center, and tail extremes",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
### There does not seem to be many outliers. The difference in rounds and total line up becasuse the total will be less if there is less rounds.

# PART 3


# Decision Tree
## Tree Preperation
```{r}

tree_data <- pga_master %>%
  inner_join(course_data, by = c("course_name" = "course")) %>%
  select(
    cut_status,
    sg_ott,
    sg_app,
    sg_arg,
    sg_putt,
    adj_driving_distance) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(cut_status = as.factor(cut_status))
```

## Training Data and Fitting Model
```{r}
set.seed(888)

data_split <- initial_split(tree_data, prop = 0.80, strata = cut_status)

train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data  <- testing(data_split)

train_data_pretty <- train_data %>%
  rename(
    `SG: Off the Tee`         = sg_ott,
    `SG: Approach`            = sg_app,
    `SG: Around the Green`    = sg_arg,
    `SG: Putting`             = sg_putt,
    `Course Driving Distance` = adj_driving_distance)

tree_fit <- tree_spec %>%
  fit(cut_status ~ ., data = train_data_pretty)
```

## Tree Visualization
```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=10}
tree_fit %>%
  extract_fit_engine() %>%
  rpart.plot(
    type = 4,
    extra = 104,
    under = TRUE,
    faclen = 0,
    main = "Decision Tree: PGA Tour Cut Status")
```
## Evaluating Fit
```{r}
test_data_pretty <- test_data %>%
  rename(
    `SG: Off the Tee`         = sg_ott,
    `SG: Approach`            = sg_app,
    `SG: Around the Green`    = sg_arg,
    `SG: Putting`             = sg_putt,
    `Course Driving Distance` = adj_driving_distance)

results <- test_data_pretty %>%
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit, test_data_pretty)) %>%
  bind_cols(predict(tree_fit, test_data_pretty, type = "prob"))

results %>%
  conf_mat(truth = cut_status, estimate = .pred_class)

results %>%
  metrics(truth = cut_status, estimate = .pred_class)
```

## Hyperparameter Tuning
```{r}
tune_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  min_n = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("rpart") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(123)
folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = cut_status)

tune_res <- tune_grid(
  tune_spec,
  cut_status ~ .,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = 10)

best_tree <- tune_res %>%
  select_best(metric = "accuracy")

final_fit <- tune_spec %>%
  finalize_model(best_tree) %>%
  fit(cut_status ~ ., data = train_data)
```

## Plotting the Tuned Tree
```{r}

fit_engine <- extract_fit_engine(final_fit)

var_map <- c(
  "sg_ott"               = "SG: Off the Tee",
  "sg_app"               = "SG: Approach",
  "sg_arg"               = "SG: Around the Green",
  "sg_putt"              = "SG: Putting",
  "adj_driving_distance" = "Course Driving Distance")

fit_engine$frame$var <- ifelse(
  fit_engine$frame$var %in% names(var_map),
  var_map[fit_engine$frame$var],
  fit_engine$frame$var)

rpart.plot(
  fit_engine,
  type = 4,
  extra = 104,
  under = TRUE,
  faclen = 0,
  main = "Tuned Decision Tree: PGA Tour Cut Status")
```

## Analysis Approach
To predict whether a PGA Tour player will make or miss the cut based on player performance metrics and course characteristics, we implement a supervised learning. The analysis is set up using the tidymodels to ensure a good modeling workflow. First, we set a seed to ensure complete reproducibility. The dataset is split into an 80% training set and a 20% testing set using sampling on the target variable (cut_status). To guard against overfitting and reliably evaluate model generalization, we employ 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. For model optimization, hyperparameter tuning focuses on decision tree complexity using grid search (tune_grid()), evaluating variations in cost_complexity, tree_depth, and min_n across 10 candidate parameter combinations to maximize classification accuracy and area under the ROC curve (ROC AUC).

### Setting up the Data

```{r}
model_data <- pga_master %>%
  inner_join(course_data, by = c("course_name" = "course")) %>%
  select(
    cut_status,
    sg_ott,
    sg_app,
    sg_arg,
    sg_putt,
    adj_driving_distance
  ) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(cut_status = factor(cut_status, levels = c("Made Cut", "Missed Cut")))

set.seed(888)
data_split <- initial_split(model_data, prop = 0.80, strata = cut_status)
train_data <- training(data_split)
test_data  <- testing(data_split)
```

## Baseline Fit
```{r}
baseline_recipe <- recipe(cut_status ~ sg_ott + sg_app, data = train_data)

baseline_spec <- logistic_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glm") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

baseline_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(baseline_recipe) %>%
  add_model(baseline_spec)

baseline_fit <- baseline_wf %>% fit(data = train_data)

baseline_results <- test_data %>%
  bind_cols(predict(baseline_fit, test_data)) %>%
  bind_cols(predict(baseline_fit, test_data, type = "prob"))

baseline_results %>%
  metrics(truth = cut_status, estimate = .pred_class)

conf_mat(baseline_results, truth = cut_status, estimate = .pred_class)
```
### Baseline Model Analysis
For our baseline model, we fitted a binary logistic regression predicting cut status using core golf metrics: Strokes Gained Off-the-Tee Strokes Gained on approach 

On the test dataset (259 observations), the baseline model achieved an accuracy of ~79.5%. While the model correctly identified 184 players who made the cut, it struggled significantly with identifying players who missed the cut—misclassifying 42 missed-cut players as having made the cut (False Positives) and only correctly identifying 22 missed cuts. This baseline demonstrates that while long-game hitting stats offers initial predictive power, linear golf metrics alone are insufficient for classifying cut-line decisions.


## Advanced Model Fit
```{r}

tree_recipe <- recipe(
  cut_status ~ sg_ott + sg_app + sg_arg + sg_putt + adj_driving_distance, 
  data = train_data
)

tune_spec <- decision_tree(
  cost_complexity = tune(),
  tree_depth = tune(),
  min_n = tune()
) %>%
  set_engine("rpart") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

tune_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(tree_recipe) %>%
  add_model(tune_spec)

set.seed(888)
folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = cut_status)

tune_res <- tune_grid(
  tune_wf,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = 10,
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy, roc_auc)
)

best_tree <- tune_res %>% select_best(metric = "accuracy")
final_wf <- tune_wf %>% finalize_workflow(best_tree)
final_fit <- final_wf %>% fit(data = train_data)

tree_results <- test_data %>%
  bind_cols(predict(final_fit, test_data)) %>%
  bind_cols(predict(final_fit, test_data, type = "prob"))

tree_results %>%
  metrics(truth = cut_status, estimate = .pred_class)

conf_mat(tree_results, truth = cut_status, estimate = .pred_class)
```
### Advanced Fit Analysis
To capture non-linear relationships and short-game dynamics, we expanded our feature set to include short-game performance (Strokes Gained Around-the-Green `sg_arg` and Strokes Gained on Putting `sg_putt`) alongside course characteristics (`adj_driving_distance`). We trained a Decision Tree (`decision_tree()`) engine using `rpart` and tuned hyperparameters across a v = 5, 5-fold cross-validation.

Hyperparameter tuning selected a good parameter set that balanced tree depth and split thresholds to prevent overfitting. On the test set, the advanced model significantly improved detection of missed cuts, correctly identifying 42 missed-cut players while maintaining high overall accuracy (~83.8%). Integrating short-game performance and course-level factors allowed the decision tree to capture non-linear thresholds where strong putting or other on the field playing compensates for average driving distance.

## Model Evaluation

```{r}

fit_engine <- extract_fit_engine(final_fit)

var_map <- c(
  "sg_ott"               = "SG: Off the Tee",
  "sg_app"               = "SG: Approach",
  "sg_arg"               = "SG: Around Green",
  "sg_putt"              = "SG: Putting",
  "adj_driving_distance" = "Course Driving Distance"
)

fit_engine$frame$var <- ifelse(
  fit_engine$frame$var %in% names(var_map),
  var_map[fit_engine$frame$var],
  fit_engine$frame$var
)

rpart.plot(
  fit_engine,
  type = 4,
  extra = 104,
  under = TRUE,
  faclen = 0,
  roundint = FALSE,
  main = "Tuned Decision Tree Structure for PGA Tour Cut Status"
)
```
## ROC Curve Comparison
```{r}
bind_rows(
  baseline_results %>% mutate(model = "Baseline (Logistic)"),
  tree_results %>% mutate(model = "Advanced (Tuned Tree)")
) %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  roc_curve(truth = cut_status, `.pred_Made Cut`) %>%
  autoplot() +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curve Comparison: Baseline vs. Advanced Decision Tree",
    subtitle = "Trade-offs between True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate",
    x = "1 - Specificity (False Positive Rate)",
    y = "Sensitivity (True Positive Rate)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```
### Model Evaluation Analysis
 This plot compares how good the baseline fit is (blue) and hwo goo the Advanced tree is (red). It is players who made the cut across all variables.
The ROC curve comparison demonstrates that the Advanced Tuned Decision Tree outperforms the Baseline Logistic Regression across most probability thresholds. By achieving a larger Area Under the Curve, the decision tree proves that integrating short-game metrics (sg_putt, sg_arg) and course characteristics alongside hyperparameter tuning gives better classification compared to relying only on linear golf metrics.

## 4. Model Evaluation & ROC Curve Comparison

The ROC curve comparison demonstrates that the Advanced Tuned Decision Tree outperforms the Baseline Logistic Regression across most probability thresholds. By achieving a higher Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC), the decision tree confirms that integrating short-game metrics (`sg_putt`, `sg_arg`) and course-adjusted distance alongside non-linear hyperparameter tuning yields superior predictive performance compared to simple linear ball-striking models.

### Model Error Analysis & Limitations

Despite these improvements, systematic classification errors remain on the cut boundary:

False Positives (22 instances)

False Negatives (20 instances)

### Limitations
PGA Tour cut lines are highly sensitive to dynamic, unmodeled variables such as weather changes, player fatigue, and pressure. Future iterations should incorporate player historical performance on specific course setups and multi-round scoring variance.
